This paper introduces EVAAA, a novel 3D virtual environment for training and evaluating reinforcement learning agents based on the biological concept of homeostasis. Instead of relying on externally defined, task-specific rewards, agents in EVAAA are driven by the need to maintain internal "essential variables"—such as satiation, hydration, and body temperature—within viable bounds. This principled approach allows for the autonomous emergence of goals and complex survival behaviors. The platform is well-designed, featuring a curriculum of increasingly difficult survival environments for training and a separate suite of experimental testbeds for evaluating generalization and specific cognitive capabilities like planning and exploration.

The core strength of EVAAA lies in its elegant and biologically-grounded intrinsic reward system, which moves away from brittle, handcrafted rewards common in RL. Reviewers uniformly praised this conceptual foundation, the high quality of the benchmark's design and implementation on Unity ML-Agents, the clarity of the paper, and the thoughtful evaluation structure. The inclusion of multimodal sensory inputs and egocentric embodiment further enhances the platform's realism and relevance for studying autonomous and adaptive agents.

Initial reviews identified several areas for improvement. A key point of discussion was the need to more explicitly connect the homeostatic motivation to the evaluation of broader RL capabilities like planning and exploration. Other weaknesses included the lack of stronger, memory-equipped model-free baselines (e.g., PPO+LSTM) to compare against the model-based DreamerV3, the absence of a direct comparison against an agent trained with traditional extrinsic rewards, and a relatively simple agent action space that limits the complexity of emergent strategies.

The authors provided a constructive and thoughtful rebuttal, agreeing with the reviewers' suggestions. They committed to clarifying the benchmark's utility for evaluating core RL competencies beyond homeostasis in the final version. They also pledged to include experiments with stronger memory-based baselines and a direct comparison to an extrinsic reward paradigm, and to create a "pure planning" testbed to better isolate this capability. While these additions will appear in the camera-ready version, the authors' positive engagement and clear plan for strengthening the paper addressed the reviewers' concerns, leading them to maintain their positive scores.

We thank the Reviewer for providing constructive feedback. Below, we address each comment in detail.

-----

**R3-1:** ***“Incomplete Algorithmic Baselines: The comparison between the complex, model-based DreamerV3 and simple, memory-less model-free agents (DQN, PPO) is insufficient. As EVAAA is a POMDP, a more conclusive comparison would require testing against stronger model-free baselines equipped with memory, such as Recurrent PPO (PPO+LSTM), which are known to be competitive in such environments.”***

**Response:** We agree with the reviewer that recurrent, memory-equipped baselines are highly relevant for EVAAA, which is inherently a partially observable environment. At the same time, we would like to kindly clarify that the primary goal of this work was to introduce EVAAA as an environment with an appropriate level of complexity—challenging enough to elicit meaningful autonomous and adaptive behaviors, but not so difficult that learning becomes infeasible—rather than to provide an exhaustive algorithmic benchmark.Thus, we chose to use DreamerV3, as it was state-of-the-art at the time of development and particularly well-suited to EVAAA’s complexity: its model-based design incorporates memory and planning through a world model, making it an appropriate reference point for evaluating EVAAA.

Nevertheless, we fully agree with the reviewer that RL researchers will have a strong interest in comparisons with model-free baselines that incorporate memory. To address this, although we are unable to provide these results during the rebuttal period due to the committee’s policy, we will include Recurrent PPO results in the camera-ready version.

----

**R3-2:** ***Lack of Direct Reward Paradigm Comparison: The paper's core premise is that its intrinsic, homeostatic reward system is superior to brittle, extrinsic rewards. However, the experiments do not include a direct comparison against a baseline agent trained with a well-designed extrinsic reward function within the EVAAA environment (e.g., providing a direct positive reward for approaching the food when hungry). Such an experiment would more empirically demonstrate the claimed behavioral benefits of the intrinsic approach over a traditional one.***

**Response:** We fully agree that a direct comparison between agents training with intrinsic vs. extrinsic reward would provide valuable evidence for understanding the relative benefits of intrinsic rewards. We also acknowledge that our current manuscript does not fully address this comparison. While we are unable to add new experimental results during the rebuttal period due to the committee’s policy, we will prepare and include a direct comparison in the camera-ready version of the paper. 

It is important to note, however, that a fully “fair” comparison may not be feasible, as any modification will alter the task difficulty—which was a key reason for our hesitation to include such comparisons in the present manuscript. For example, providing direct rewards for approaching and consuming resources may encourage the agent to rely on isolated behaviors (e.g., staying near a food source) rather than learning to coordinate across multiple internal needs. Further, if we retain the homeostatic framework but withhold information about the essential variables, the task becomes substantially more difficult, as there is no way for the agent to learn the causal link between its actions and death.

While a perfectly balanced comparison may not be achievable, we believe that even a simplified version of comparisons could add meaningful insights to the study. In the camera-ready version, we will incorporate extrinsic reward settings—such as providing a direct positive reward for approaching food when hungry or for consuming resources—and compare these agents within the experimental testbed. This will help us examine how different reward conditions, intrinsic versus extrinsic, influence the emergence of more autonomous and adaptive behaviors.

----

**R3-3:** ***Oversimplified Agent Actions: The agent's action space is limited to simple navigation and eating. This restricts the complexity of survival strategies that can emerge and be studied, limiting the benchmark's fidelity to real-world challenges that often require manipulation or more complex interactions.***

**Response:** We agree with the reviewer that the current action space is minimalistic (i.e., move forward, turn, eat), and this naturally limits the range of survival strategies that can emerge. However, this relatively simple action design reflects our intention to prioritize reproducibility, training stability, and a clear baseline for evaluating survival strategy before introducing more complex behaviors.Furthermore, starting with a simple agent allowed us to focus on calibrating the difficulty of EVAAA’s environments. For example, during development, even this simplified agent struggled with some of the high-level tasks (e.g., level 3-2, see Fig. 4), and thus, our initial priority was to calibrate environment complexity.

However, we fully agree with the reviewer’s comment that increasing action complexity will broaden EVAAA’s utility for RL research. We are planning to integrate more complex agent embodiments supported by Unity ML-Agents in future studies—such as the Crawler quadruped, a creature with four arms and four forearms that already provides a locomotion model with multiple joints and more realistic movement dynamics. Incorporating agents like the Crawler will enable richer survival strategies and open the door to tasks involving more advanced forms of navigation and interaction. At the same time, we will retain the simpler agent as a reproducible baseline. This approach will expand EVAAA’s scope, allowing researchers to study both foundational RL behaviors and more complex, embodied interaction strategies within the same benchmark. In the camera-ready version of the paper, we will add this to the limitation with future direction as below.

**Suggested revision (This will be added to Chapter 10 “Conclusion and Limitations”):** *While EVAAA currently uses a simplified agent with a basic action space (move forward, turn, eat) to ensure reproducibility and training stability, future iterations will integrate more complex Unity ML-Agents embodiments such as the Crawler quadruped—a creature with four arms and four forearms—while retaining the simpler agent as a reproducible baseline.*

We thank the Reviewers for your positive evaluation of our study and for the thoughtful comments. To the best of our understanding, your comments touch on the following three important aspects: (1) whether the homeostatic reward might inadvertently bias the agent toward simpler behaviors rather than more complex high-order cognitive ones, such as exploration or planning; (2) how EVAAA could better demonstrate its relevance as a benchmark for evaluating RL algorithms beyond homeostatic regulation; and (3) whether test cases could be refined to better isolate planning from other confounding elements. Below, we address each comment in detail. 

----

**R1-1:** ***“Conceptually the homeostatic balancing is multi-objective RL. The reward defined seems to be a reasonable method of achieving sufficient balance, but it is creating a biased dense reward out of the environment objective of maintaining sufficient resources to complete an episode.”***

**Response:** We agree that the homeostatic balancing problem posed by EVAAA can be naturally framed as a multi-objective RL task, as agents must regulate multiple essential variables simultaneously. Our current reward design—based on continuous feedback from internal state variables—offers a practical solution to facilitate learning in complex, partially observable environments. 

We also acknowledge the Reviewer’s concern that such a dense reward may bias learning toward simple heuristic solutions. However, the reward structure in EVAAA does not trivialize the task—even with ongoing dense feedback from internal states, this information alone does not necessarily lead to success. For instance, unlike the simpler environments such as Level 1-1 and Level 1-2, where resources are easily visible, Levels 2-1 and 2-2 require the agent to avoid obstacles and locate resources hidden among nearby trees (Fig. 3a). Level 3-1 further challenges the agent by requiring it to remember the spatial locations of resources obscured by walls, demanding navigation and memory. The results show that the agent can perform effectively in these levels, demonstrating that it engages in higher-order cognitive processes such as navigation and memory (Fig. 4a).

Moreover, we would like to point out that EVAAA does not necessarily need to be framed only as a continuous reward design. For example, the agent could receive zero reward upon death and a constant reward for all other steps, or alternatively, a large negative reward for death only and zero reward for all other steps. Because EVAAA’s reward function is modular, switching between continuous and sparse reward structures requires only minor adjustments. To reflect the Reviewer’s concern, we will include a description of this sparse-reward configuration in the camera-ready version.

-----

**R1-2:** ***“It would be helpful to more clearly discuss how the benchmark would enable better evaluation of RL algorithms. From my understanding this benchmark could be useful to evaluating an agent's planning capabilities and potentially exploration (although this is not examined in this paper). Much of the discussion is in regard to homeostatic balancing, which while interesting as a motivation, the relevance to RL evaluation is less clear.”***

**Response:** Thank you for this important point. EVAAA was initially developed based on the idea that intrinsic, homeostatic rewards can drive agents—similar to animals—to exhibit autonomous and adaptive behavior. However, as we built the environment, we quickly realized that maintaining homeostasis in a complex and dynamic environment requires a range of cognitive capabilities, including navigation, exploration, and planning. This led us to design more challenging survival task levels. For example, Level 3-1 (navigation) requires the agent to map and move through a semi-structured terrain. Level 3-2 (exploration) demands that the agent search for resources whose locations change over time. Level 4-1 (predator threat) requires the agent to balance survival needs with threat avoidance under dynamically changing conditions. Notably, our training results indicate that survival in such complex environments demands more advanced cognitive capabilities, such as planning and exploration. For example, the agent exhibits a significant performance drop beyond Level 3-2 (Fig. 4a), suggesting that simply relying on homeostatic regulation is insufficient and that agents must develop more sophisticated cognitive functions. From a generalization perspective, training solely on early-stage environments like Levels 1-1 and 1-2 fails to prepare agents for even seemingly simple evaluation tasks, such as the two-resource choice (water) task (Fig. 4b). In contrast, exposure to more complex levels (Levels 2-1 through 4-1) enables the agent to develop richer representations and policies needed for adaptive behavior in novel situations. These results highlight that achieving high performance in advanced survival environments and experimental testbeds requires agents not only to regulate homeostasis as a ‘motivational’ driver, but also to develop higher-order cognitive functions such as exploration, memory, generalization, goal manipulation, and planning.

Given this context, we fully agree with the Reviewer that EVAAA’s relevance to RL evaluation needs to be generalized more than just homeostatic motivation. In fact, our original goal was for EVAAA to serve not merely as a model of biological behavior, but indeed as a benchmark for evaluating core RL capabilities. For example, Level 3-2 was explicitly designed to evaluate exploration ability, as resources do not spawn in fixed locations. Similarly, the Multi-Goal Planning and Y-maze testbeds were developed to assess planning and spatial navigation abilities, requiring the agent to prioritize resource consumption and sequence actions based on its internal state.

Admitting that our original manuscript might not have fully conveyed this intention, our revision  explicitly highlighted how EVAAA can be used to evaluate a spectrum of RL algorithms—including exploration, planning, navigation, and generalization—extending beyond its original emphasis on homeostatic balancing, as below:

**Suggested revision (This will be added to Chapter 5):** *While these levels were initially designed to elicit biologically inspired behaviors under internal-state regulation, they also serve as targeted evaluations of core RL capabilities. For example, Level 3-2 emphasizes exploration by requiring agents to search for dynamically relocated resources in the absence of fixed cues, while Level 3-1 demands spatial navigation and path planning in semi-structured environments. Level 4-1 introduces an adversarial threat that forces agents to plan strategically to avoid a predator while still securing essential resources. Overall, these scenarios extend EVAAA’s relevance beyond homeostatic control, providing a diverse evaluation for assessing exploration strategies, planning capabilities, and generalization performance of RL agents.*

-----

**R1-3:** ***The test cases combine generalization from irrelevant aspects of the state with planning. Evaluation could be improved by including a test case in which many of the irrelevant state aspects are retained such that the planning portion of the test is isolated.***

**Response:** We appreciate this insightful suggestion. As the Reviewer pointed out, we recognize the value of a “pure planning” testbed that can isolate planning learned from the training tasks. Such testbeds would preserve many of the same visual and environmental cues but eliminate extraneous sources of generalization pressure. For example, we could present the agent with a visually similar environment in which all resources are visible and have fixed locations. Then, we can make its survival depend entirely on executing an optimal sequence of resource consumption or internal regulation to maintain homeostasis over time, based on the current levels of essential variables. 

A key strength of EVAAA is its modular configuration structure, which makes creating such targeted testing scenarios easy and straightforward. By adjusting a small number of configuration files (e.g., setting obstacle prefabs and their materials), we can easily create and share this “planning-only” condition. In response to the reviewer’s comment, we will add this pure planning testbed as a pre-set configuration in the camera-ready version, as we are not allowed to modify the code during this rebuttal stage. This addition will not only clarify the benchmark’s ability to evaluate planning as a standalone capability but will also strengthen EVAAA’s utility as a flexible and extensible tool for RL researchers who want to assess different cognitive abilities in isolation.

We thank the Reviewer for carefully examining our work and for providing thoughtful comments. We understood that your comments focus on the following three key areas: (1) the importance of testing the contribution of each sensory modality through ablation, (2) the value of extending EVAAA to support deeper cognitive tasks such as social interaction, memory, and inference, and (3) the benefit of situating EVAAA more clearly alongside benchmarks like Avalon and Crafter. Below, we responded to each comment in detail.

-----

**R2-1:** ***No ablations on individual modalities (e.g., how important is thermoception?)***

**Response:** Thank you for the constructive suggestion. We will add ablation results by systematically removing each modality in EVAAA’s environment in the camera-ready version.  

When designing EVAAA, we intentionally included multiple sensory modalities—vision, thermoception, olfaction, and collision—because we envisioned EVAAA as a benchmark for research on embodied agents, such as robots or animals, that must maintain their own “bodily health” (e.g., regulating temperature, avoiding damage). Even though not every modality directly corresponds to current robotic implementations (e.g., olfaction) or to physically realistic sensors, we focused on their core functional roles rather than replicating the full engineering detail. These multimodal sensory inputs are capable of offering stable, persistent signals even when visual cues vary dramatically across environments—a feature that distinguishes EVAAA from conventional RL benchmarks, which rarely provide a consistent source of information in changing conditions. For example, while the appearance of naturalistic training scenes may differ significantly from experimental testbeds, information from thermoception or collision sensors remains consistent. This allows agents to build stable value representations that generalize across visual variation and support emergent autonomous and adaptive behaviors—similar to how Lee et al. [1] demonstrated that relying solely on stable proprioceptive feedback enabled quadrupedal robots to robustly generalize locomotion to challenging, unseen terrains like mud, snow, and vegetation.

Nevertheless, as noted earlier, we fully agree that systematic ablation tests will provide valuable insights about the contributions of each modality. We are committed to including these ablation experiments in the camera-ready version to more clearly illustrate the role and importance of each sensory modality within EVAAA.

[1] Lee, Joonho, Jemin Hwangbo, Lorenz Wellhausen, Vladlen Koltun, and Marco Hutter. 2020. “Learning Quadrupedal Locomotion over Challenging Terrain.” Science Robotics 5 (47). https://doi.org/10.1126/scirobotics.abc5986.

-----------
**R2-2:** ***Considering deeper task types (social, memory, inference) will be good.***

**Response:** Thank you for the suggestion. We agree that extending EVAAA to encompass higher-order task types—such as social interaction, memory-based reasoning, and inference—is a natural and important next step. In this initial release, we focused on establishing foundational survival scenarios, as agents already struggled with several baseline challenges (e.g., Level 3–2). This highlights the need to stabilize and validate the core framework before scaling to more cognitively demanding tasks.

At the same time, EVAAA’s architecture was deliberately designed to support such expansion. Its modular configuration structure and Unity ML-Agents enable multi-agent setups for social tasks and support the incorporation of memory mechanisms, among other features. For example, we envision future tasks in which an agent must cooperate or compete with others for survival or remember the location of resources within a more complex terrain. These kinds of challenges would naturally extend EVAAA’s current scope by linking internal state regulation to richer social, memory, and reasoning behaviors. In our revision, we will include a discussion on these expansion ideas as a potential future direction. 

**Suggested revision: (This will be added to Chapter 10 “Conclusion and Limitations,” after the first paragraph):** *Looking ahead, EVAAA’s architecture was deliberately designed to support the addition of richer, higher-order task types beyond the current version. Because EVAAA is built on a modular Unity ML-Agents framework, it can readily accommodate advanced training and testing settings, such as multi-agent scenarios for studying cooperation or competition (i.e., social tasks), memory-dependent reasoning (e.g., recalling resource locations across changing terrains), and inference-based tasks (e.g., inferring predators’ future locations). These future expansions will extend EVAAA’s focus from survival to more complex cognitive behaviors, linking internal-state regulation to advanced capabilities such as social functioning, memory-based planning, and context-sensitive decision-making.*

-----------
**R2-3:** ***Could have compared to Avalon or Crafter on a few overlapping settings for better positioning.***

**Response:** We agree that direct comparisons with existing platforms such as Avalon and Crafter would help clarify the unique contributions and contextual relevance of EVAAA. While we did not include direct empirical comparisons in the current version, this was a deliberate decision. It is because these environments were each developed with distinct goals and assumptions, which makes aligning evaluation protocols challenging in practice. For instance, Crafter operates in a discrete 2D world with handcrafted pixel-based features and task-specific progression, whereas EVAAA focuses on continuous 3D embodiment with multimodal perception and multi-dimensional internal states. Avalon, while more similar in terms of 3D embodiment, adopts a unimodal input structure and reduces survival to a single scalar energy variable while EVAAA is built around balancing multiple internal state variables (e.g., satiation, hydration, temperature, damage), each sensed through separate perceptual channels. 

To help clarify these differences, we will add a description about the comparisons among the existing platforms in the camera-ready version to explicitly position unique points of EVAAA alongside those from Avalon and Crafter. This comparison will highlight how EVAAA expands survival-based benchmarks by enabling broader investigations into adaptive, internal-state driven behavior in embodied agents.

**Suggested revision (This will be added to Chapter 3 “Survival Environments” section):** *In contrast, EVAAA offers a 3D multimodal framework with explicit, multi-dimensional internal states. These distinctions position EVAAA as a complementary benchmark that broadens the design space for survival environments by enabling richer evaluation of adaptive behavior and internal-state-driven control.*

summary.value: This paper proposes EVAAA, a biologically-inspired 3D simulation benchmark where reinforcement learning agents regulate internal physiological states (e.g., hydration, satiation, body temperature, damage) to survive in dynamic environments. EVAAA integrates curriculum-based training environments and a suite of experimental testbeds, uses multimodal egocentric perception, and evaluates autonomy and adaptivity via internal-variable-driven behavior.

strengths_contributions.value:
- Biological grounding: Homeostatic regulation as reward signal is elegant and meaningful. It allows goal emergence from internal dynamics instead of hardcoded reward engineering.

- Benchmark quality: Includes diverse environments, clear curriculum, egocentric multimodal perception (vision, thermoception, olfaction, etc.), and structured testbeds with meaningful generalization tasks.

- Evaluation: Solid. DreamerV3 vs PPO vs DQN across levels, human comparisons, curriculum vs non-curriculum training. Plots are clear and honest (e.g., failures at higher levels).

- Design: Environment is well-structured, customizable, and cleanly built on Unity ML-Agents.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
- No ablations on individual modalities (e.g., how important is thermoception?)

- Considering deeper task types (social, memory, inference) will be good.

- Could have compared to Avalon or Crafter on a few overlapping settings for better positioning.

summary.value:
This paper presents EVAAA, a 3D simulation benchmark for RL, with the following primary contributions:

1. It introduces a framework where agents are driven by internal homeostatic needs instead of external rewards. An intrinsic reward signal is generated from the agent's regulation of *Essential Variables* like satiation, hydration, and temperature.
2. It provides a two-tiered evaluation architecture, consisting of a progressive training curriculum to learn survival behaviors and a separate suite of controlled testbeds to measure generalization.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. **Principled Intrinsic Reward Design:** The paper's core contribution is its unified intrinsic reward system based on biological homeostasis. This replaces the brittle, handcrafted external rewards common in traditional RL .
2. **Well-Designed Two-Tiered Evaluation Architecture:** The platform uniquely features a "training curriculum" for learning complex survival skills and a separate "experimental testbed" for the precise, quantitative evaluation of generalization and specific adaptive abilities .
3. **Excellent Presentation:** The paper is well-organized and clearly written. Its figures (e.g., Fig. 1, Fig. 3) are highly informative and intuitive, greatly enhancing the understanding of the platform's design and experimental workflow.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. **Incomplete Algorithmic Baselines:** The comparison between the complex, model-based DreamerV3 and simple, memory-less model-free agents (DQN, PPO) is insufficient. As EVAAA is a POMDP, a more conclusive comparison would require testing against stronger model-free baselines equipped with memory, such as Recurrent PPO (PPO+LSTM), which are known to be competitive in such environments.
2. **Lack of Direct Reward Paradigm Comparison:** The paper's core premise is that its intrinsic, homeostatic reward system is superior to brittle, extrinsic rewards. However, the experiments do not include a direct comparison against a baseline agent trained with a well-designed extrinsic reward function within the EVAAA environment (e.g., providing a direct positive reward for approaching the food when hungry). Such an experiment would more empirically demonstrate the claimed behavioral benefits of the intrinsic approach over a traditional one.
3. **Oversimplified Agent Actions:** The agent's action space is limited to simple navigation and eating. This restricts the complexity of survival strategies that can emerge and be studied, limiting the benchmark's fidelity to real-world challenges that often require manipulation or more complex interactions.

title.value: EVAAA: A Virtual Environment Platform for Essential Variables in Autonomous and Adaptive Agents

TLDR.value: We developed a novel virtual environment platform for building and testing autonomous and adaptive agents by incorporating a biologically inspired homeostatic concept of internal environment states and essential variables.

abstract.value: Reinforcement learning (RL) agents have demonstrated strong performance in structured environments, yet they continue to struggle in real-world settings where goals are ambiguous, conditions change dynamically, and external supervision is limited. These challenges stem not primarily from the algorithmic limitations but from the characteristics of conventional training environments, which are usually static, task-specific, and externally defined. In contrast, biological agents develop autonomy and adaptivity by interacting with complex, dynamic environments, where most behaviors are ultimately driven by internal physiological needs. Inspired by these biological constraints, we introduce EVAAA (Essential Variables in Autonomous and Adaptive Agents), a 3D virtual environment for training and evaluating egocentric RL agents endowed with internal physiological state variables. In EVAAA, agents must maintain essential variables (EVs)—e.g., satiation, hydration, body temperature, and tissue integrity (the level of damage)—within viable bounds by interacting with environments that increase in difficulty at each stage. The reward system is derived from internal state dynamics, enabling agents to generate goals autonomously without manually engineered, task-specific reward functions. Built on Unity ML-Agents, EVAAA supports multimodal sensory inputs, including vision, olfaction, thermoception, collision, as well as egocentric embodiment. It features naturalistic survival environments for curricular training and a suite of unseen experimental testbeds, allowing for the evaluation of autonomous and adaptive behaviors that emerge from the interplay between internal state dynamics and environmental constraints. By integrating physiological regulation, embodiment, continual learning, and generalization, EVAAA offers a biologically inspired benchmark for studying autonomy, adaptivity, and internally driven control in RL agents. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/cocoanlab/evaaa

croissant_file.description: If you checked the Dataset Submission box, upload a Croissant metadata file that documents your dataset. If your submission has more than one Croissant metadata file, please package all files into a single ZIP archive and upload it here. **Before uploading, verify that your file is valid using the [Croissant validator](https://huggingface.co/spaces/JoaquinVanschoren/croissant-checker).** If you left the Dataset Submission box unchecked, leave this field empty.

dataset_URL.description: If you checked the Dataset Submission box, provide the URL to your dataset here. **Before including the URL for your dataset, verify that you followed the [NeurIPS2025 data hosting guidelines](https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2025/DataHostingGuidelines) (as part of the CFPs) and that the URL is accessible to NeurIPS2025 reviewers.** If you left the Dataset Submission box unchecked, leave this field empty.

dataset_final_confirmation.description: **By checking this box, you confirm that: (1)** your dataset is complete and finalized at the time of submission; **(2)** you included a valid Croissant metadata file that has been verified using the [Croissant validator](https://huggingface.co/spaces/luisoala/croissant-checker); **(3)** you followed the [NeurIPS2025 data hosting guidelines](https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2025/DataHostingGuidelines); **(4)** you provided a URL pointing to the dataset that is accessible for NeurIPS2025 reviewers. If you left the Dataset Submission box unchecked, leave this box unchecked.

checklist_confirmation.description: In order to improve the rigor and transparency of research submitted to and published at NeurIPS, authors are required to complete a paper checklist and include it in the paper PDF. See [https://neurips.cc/public/guides/PaperChecklist](https://neurips.cc/public/guides/PaperChecklist) and the provided 2025 sample LaTeX file. **Papers not including the checklist in the paper PDF will be desk rejected.**

enum.description: I confirm that I have included a paper checklist in the paper PDF.

code_URL.description: If your submission includes code, provide the URL to a hosting platform (e.g., Github, Bitbucket) as described in the CFPs. See the main track [code guidelines](https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for details.

supplementary_material.description: All supplementary material must be self-contained and zipped into a single file. Note that supplementary material will be visible to reviewers throughout and after the review period, and **ensure all your supplementary material is anonymized if your submission is anonymized.** The maximum file size is 100MB. Supplementary material can be updated until the supplementary material deadline (May 22).

financial_support.description: Optionally indicate one student author on the paper who would need financial support to attend and present at the conference if the paper is accepted (or leave blank if financial support is not needed). Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors.

reviewer_nomination.description: Every submission must nominate at least one author who is a qualified reviewer (i.e., satisfying our reviewer nomination criteria [https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/](https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/) ). Being named as such a reviewer in the submission constitutes an acceptance and a commitment to carry out the regular reviewing load (~6 papers) responsibly if asked by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. Only if no qualified reviewer exists in the author list, nominate the best-qualified author for consideration by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. In addition, note that any author listed on 4 or more papers will be automatically regarded as a reviewer unless they are already serving as a reviewer, AC, SAC, or other roles in the Organization Committee. Failure to assign a qualified reviewer when one is available in the author list may result in desk rejection. Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors (separate by comma if more than one nominations).

responsible_reviewing.description: We acknowledge that every author on the program committee is obligated to conduct responsible reviewing according to the policy designed by the PC Chairs and relevant members of the organizing committee. **Failure to do so may result in desk rejection or other serious consequences.**
